title: The Lamp at Merrow Point
subtitle: On keeping a light through a long winter

content.text: On keeping a light through a long winter

The lamp turned once every eight seconds, and I had long since stopped counting the beats between. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

Fog came up the channel that morning the way smoke fills a room no one thinks to leave. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

From the gallery the sea looked less like water than like a great grey animal breathing in its sleep. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

I kept the log in a hand steadier than my nerves, because the log would outlast both of us. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

A ship passed close enough that I heard her bell before I saw her, which is its own kind of warning. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company.

The oil ran low twice that winter, and twice I walked the six miles to the store rather than let the light fail. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both.

There is a particular silence that follows a wreck, and it is not the silence of peace. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

My predecessor left a note pinned inside the lamp room door: mind the wind, it changes its mind before you do. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac.

On clear nights the beam swept the water like a hand searching a dark room for a dropped key. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own.

I have come to think of the tower less as a building than as a very patient argument against the dark. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable.

The gulls nested in the rock below and complained, as they always did, about everything at once. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be.

A letter came twice a month by the supply boat, and twice a month I read it standing at the rail. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome.

Storms here do not announce themselves; they simply arrive, the way grief arrives, mid-sentence. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

I learned to mend the winding gear myself, because the mainland was three hours away on a good sea. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.

The keeper before the keeper before me carved his initials into the stair rail, and I have never sanded them out. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

When the light held through a bad night I felt something close to pride, though pride is a poor word for it. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

The horizon at dusk turned the colour of a bruise healing, violet giving way to a tired green. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does.

I counted the ships that passed safely as another man might count blessings, which is to say I counted them at all. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late.

There is a ledger for the oil, a ledger for the weather, and no ledger at all for what the solitude costs. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.

By April the ice had gone from the rocks and the birds came back as though nothing had happened. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be.

The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time.

An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument.

The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing.

A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect.

The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first.

An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it.
